Anthracnose.description: Anthracnose is a highly destructive fungal disease in sorghum that affects leaves, stalks, and panicles.
Anthracnose.symptoms: Small, circular to oval water-soaked spots on leaves that turn reddish-brown to tan with dark borders. Small black spots (acervuli) appear in the center of lesions.
Anthracnose.causes: Caused by the fungus Colletotrichum sublineolum. It spreads through wind-borne spores, splashing rain, and infected crop residues under warm, humid conditions.
Anthracnose.treatment: Apply systemic fungicides if the infection is detected early in the crop cycle.
Anthracnose.organic_treatment: Use neem oil sprays, bio-fungicides containing Trichoderma viride or Pseudomonas fluorescens, and practice crop rotation with non-host crops.
Anthracnose.chemical_treatment: Spray Carbendazim (0.1%) or Mancozeb (0.25%) at the onset of symptoms.
Anthracnose.prevention: Grow resistant cultivars, use certified pathogen-free seeds, destroy crop residues after harvest, and maintain proper plant spacing.
Anthracnose.reference: FAO Sorghum Disease Guide / ICRISAT Plant Protection Bulletins

Cereal Grain molds.description: Grain mold is a complex disease affecting sorghum grain development, reducing grain quality, viability, and yield.
Cereal Grain molds.symptoms: Discoloration of the grain (pink, white, grey, or black molds growing on the surface of the grains) before harvest. Grains become soft and powdery.
Cereal Grain molds.causes: A fungal complex including species of Fusarium, Curvularia, Alternaria, and Bipolaris. Primarily favored by wet, humid weather during flowering and grain filling.
Cereal Grain molds.treatment: Harvest crops early as soon as physiological maturity is reached to prevent mold development.
Cereal Grain molds.organic_treatment: Apply bio-control agents like Pseudomonas fluorescens or Trichoderma harzianum at flowering stage.
Cereal Grain molds.chemical_treatment: Spray Propiconazole (0.1%) or a mixture of Carbendazim and Mancozeb during the flowering/panicle emergence stage.
Cereal Grain molds.prevention: Plant mold-resistant cultivars, schedule planting so grain maturity avoids the peak of the rainy season, and ensure quick post-harvest drying.

Covered Kernel smut.description: Covered kernel smut replaces individual grains with fungal spore sacs, leading to major grain yield loss.
Covered Kernel smut.symptoms: Grains are replaced by white to greyish cone-shaped sacs (sori) containing dark spores. The sacs remain intact until threshing.
Covered Kernel smut.causes: Caused by the fungus Sporisorium sorghi. It is a seed-borne disease where spores infect the seedling during germination.
Covered Kernel smut.treatment: Fungicidal seed treatments are highly effective and are the primary control method.
Covered Kernel smut.organic_treatment: Treat seeds with hot water or biological seed coating (e.g., Trichoderma dust). Rotate crops to minimize spore load in the soil.
Covered Kernel smut.chemical_treatment: Treat seeds with Thiram, Captan, or Carboxin at 2-3 g/kg of seed before sowing.
Covered Kernel smut.prevention: Use certified clean seeds, treat seeds before planting, and practice deep summer plowing to bury spores.

Head Smut.description: Head smut is a systemic disease that completely destroys the sorghum inflorescence, replacing the panicle with a large smut gall.
Head Smut.symptoms: The entire panicle is replaced by a large, dark brown to black spore mass covered by a thin white membrane that ruptures to release spores.
Head Smut.causes: Caused by the soil-borne fungus Sporisorium reilianum. Infection occurs at the seedling stage from soil-borne spores.
Head Smut.treatment: Remove and burn infected plants before the smut gall ruptures. Apply soil fungicides in high-value plots.
Head Smut.organic_treatment: Apply organic soil amendments (e.g., compost, biochar) to promote microbial competition against the pathogen.
Head Smut.chemical_treatment: Seed treatment with systemic fungicides like Tebuconazole or Triadimenol helps reduce seedling infection.
Head Smut.prevention: Grow head smut-resistant hybrids, practice crop rotation for at least 3 years, and maintain soil health.
Head Smut.reference: USDA Agricultural Research Service - Smut Diseases of Sorghum

Rust.description: Sorghum rust is a common foliage disease that reduces green leaf area, affecting photosynthesis and yield.
Rust.symptoms: Small, raised reddish-brown pustules (uredinia) on both upper and lower leaf surfaces. Pustules rupture to release rusty-colored spores.
Rust.causes: Caused by the fungus Puccinia purpurea. It is favored by cool, damp weather, high humidity, and heavy dew.
Rust.treatment: Apply foliar fungicides upon the first detection of rust pustules in the lower canopy.
Rust.organic_treatment: Use sulfur dusts or copper-based organic fungicides. Remove alternative hosts like Oxalis weed.
Rust.chemical_treatment: Spray Mancozeb (0.2%) or Propiconazole (0.1%) when symptoms first appear.
Rust.prevention: Plant rust-resistant cultivars, avoid high planting density to improve airflow, and eliminate weed hosts.
Rust.reference: CABI Plantwise Knowledge Bank - Sorghum Rust

healthy.description: The sorghum plant is healthy, showing normal leaf color, vigorous growth, and no visible signs of infection.
healthy.symptoms: Vibrant green leaves, uniform growth, robust stalk development, and clean developing panicles.
healthy.causes: Optimal growth conditions, balanced fertilization, proper irrigation, and effective pest/disease management.
healthy.treatment: No active treatment required. Continue standard agricultural practices.
healthy.organic_treatment: Maintain soil health using organic compost, bio-fertilizers, and scheduled crop scouting.
healthy.chemical_treatment: None needed. Avoid unnecessary chemical applications.
healthy.prevention: Regularly scout the field, maintain proper spacing, rotate crops, and optimize watering schedules.

loose smut.description: Loose smut affects the sorghum panicle, causing premature rupture of smut galls and early spore dispersal.
loose smut.symptoms: Affected plants flower earlier. Smut galls are longer, pointed, and break open easily on the plant, exposing a dark powdery mass of spores.
loose smut.causes: Caused by the fungus Sporisorium cruentum. It is a seed-borne infection that becomes systemic within the growing plant.
loose smut.treatment: Field control relies on certified disease-free seeds and chemical seed treatment.
loose smut.organic_treatment: Employ hot water seed immersion or biological seed dressing with antagonistic bacteria.
loose smut.chemical_treatment: Treat seeds with Thiram or Carboxin-Thiram mixtures at 2 g/kg seed before planting.
loose smut.prevention: Rogue out infected plants early, plant resistant crop varieties, and practice crop rotation.
loose smut.reference: Plant Pathology - Smuts of Sorghum Crops
